heading: PROPHET ISḤĀQ (AS) & PROPHET YAʿQŪB (AS)
title: A LEGACY OF FAITH
themes: Gratitude • Truth • Wise Counsel • Beautiful Patience • Hope • Tawḥīd
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 22 SELECTED AYĀT
introduction: This ninth world builds on the first eight ʿIBRAH Junior volumes, following the lives of Ādam, Idrīs, Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Ibrāhīm, Lūṭ and Ismāʿīl (peace be upon them). Its protagonists remain Imaan, Akhlaq, Salaam, Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle, Sir Zameer, Mohsin and Mohsina. The fictional family and school experiences are kept separate from the historical Qur’anic accounts.

Two Prophets share this volume because their Qur’anic lives form one family legacy: the glad tidings of Isḥāq, the gift of Yaʿqūb, their righteousness and leadership, and the remarkable counsel of Yaʿqūb as a father. We deliberately reserve the full life of Yūsuf (AS) for Volume Ten, while including the events necessary to understand Yaʿqūb’s patience and hope. The existing ʿIBRAH Junior volume on Ibrāhīm supplies continuity; the principal historical foundation here is the Qur’an itself, read with classical Tafsīr. No complete adult ʿIBRAH Isḥāq/Yaʿqūb manuscript was found in the materials available for this edition, so this is not represented as a line-by-line adaptation of one.

stories.title: The Two Names on the Family Tree
stories.subtitle: A mystery that begins with gratitude

blocks.text: The little compass from Sheikh Uncle’s library had been quiet for a week. It lay inside its ordinary case beside the blue promise folder that Imaan and Akhlaq had used during their lessons about Prophet Ismāʿīl (AS). Akhlaq had almost decided that the mystery had ended when Dadi Jaan placed a carefully folded sheet of paper on the breakfast table.
“Today,” she announced, “we are going to build a family tree.”
Akhlaq looked at the sheet suspiciously. “With actual leaves?”
“Only if you insist on watering the paper,” Imaan replied.
Dadi asked them to write the names they already knew: Ibrāhīm, Hājar, Ismāʿīl. She then drew another branch from Ibrāhīm and placed a question mark beside it. “Who belongs here?”

Neither child answered immediately. They remembered that Ibrāhīm had been given more than one son, but their recent stories had concentrated on Ismāʿīl. Dadi opened a Qur’an to Sūrat Hūd, verse 71, and explained that the wife of Ibrāhīm received glad tidings of Isḥāq, and after Isḥāq, of Yaʿqūb. These were not merely family names in an old record. Allah honoured both as prophets and among the righteous.
Akhlaq carefully wrote ISḤĀQ. Then he hesitated over YAʿQŪB. “Does this name go beside him or underneath him?”
“Underneath,” Dadi said. “Yaʿqūb is the son of Isḥāq and the grandson of Ibrāhīm. Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq are brothers.”
For several moments the children worked silently. Then Imaan noticed that Akhlaq had drawn one branch in gold and the other in pencil. “Why two colours?” she asked.
“The gold branch has the Kaʿbah story,” he said.
Dadi leaned forward. “And does a golden pencil make one branch more loved by Allah?”

Akhlaq shook his head. He had meant no harm, but suddenly saw how easily a family tree could become a competition. Allah’s prophets were honoured by revelation and righteousness, not by our favourite episode or by the colour of a chart. Dadi reminded them that the Qur’an praises both branches and that family connections carry responsibilities rather than permission to boast.
Imaan took the pencil and made the whole diagram the same colour. “We should give every name its correct place,” she said, “not turn it into a trophy cabinet.”
At the bottom of the sheet Dadi wrote a question: WHAT MAKES A FAMILY LEGACY BEAUTIFUL?

The compass did not glow. It did not open a door. It merely reflected the morning light. Yet the children had found the next mystery: not how many famous names a family contained, but what kind of faith and character those names would pass on.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Family guidance should lead to gratitude rather than comparison.

stories.title: The News Nobody Expected
stories.subtitle: Glad tidings are gifts, not guarantees we control

blocks.text: The following afternoon, Salamah returned from visiting an older neighbour who had been unwell. She brought a small pot of homemade soup that the neighbour had sent for Dadi Jaan. Akhlaq took one look at it and asked whether kindness was now being traded in containers.
“It is not a trade,” Salamah said. “She was grateful that someone remembered her.”

Imaan had been reading their family-tree notes. She asked whether Isḥāq’s birth was the same sort of ordinary happy family news that anyone might receive. Dadi Jaan said that every child is a gift, but the glad tidings to Ibrāhīm’s household belonged to a particular event related in the Qur’an. The news came when the parents were of advanced age; the account drew attention to Allah’s power and mercy. We should not invent dates, exact ages or conversations that revelation does not establish.
Akhlaq wanted to know why the Qur’an mentioned Yaʿqūb before he had even been born. “Because,” Imaan answered slowly, “the glad tidings included a future generation.”
“More than that,” Dadi added. “Allah was showing a blessing that would extend beyond one moment. But receiving a blessing does not mean we can plan every detail of the future.”

That evening, the children prepared a welcome card for a new pupil who would be joining their class. Mohsina suggested a colourful design. Akhlaq wanted to promise the pupil that the first day would be wonderful and everyone would become a friend immediately.
Imaan stopped him. “Can we really guarantee that?”
Akhlaq frowned. “I’m only trying to be nice.”
“You can be kind without promising something you cannot control,” Salamah said. “You can promise what you yourself will do: greet the child, explain the timetable and include them at lunch.”
They rewrote the card: WE WILL HELP YOU FEEL WELCOME. The difference was small but important. They could choose their effort and their manners. They could not order every feeling or every outcome.

When the new pupil arrived the next morning, everything did not go perfectly. A game was cancelled because of rain; the classroom was noisy; someone forgot the pupil’s name. But the children kept the promise that was theirs to keep. They introduced themselves, shared the class schedule and made space at the table.
At home, Akhlaq looked again at the names ISḤĀQ and YAʿQŪB. “So the lesson is not that my wishes will always happen.”
“No,” Dadi replied. “It is that Allah’s blessings deserve gratitude, and when we offer hope to someone, we should also offer honest care.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Receive blessings gratefully, without promising an outcome only Allah knows.

stories.title: Hands That Help, Eyes That Notice
stories.subtitle: Strength and insight belong together

blocks.text: At Sheikh Uncle’s Academy, the children received a challenge to create a reading corner for younger pupils. The school had donated two shelves, a few floor cushions and a box of books. Team Amanah volunteered at once.
Mohsin lifted the heavier shelf. Akhlaq hurried to fix the labels. Imaan sorted the books by reading level. Mohsina watched the doorway and noticed a problem that the others had missed.
“The shelf will block the path if we put it there,” she said.
Akhlaq shook his head. “But we’ve already carried it across the room.”
“And if someone using a walking aid needs to pass?” Mohsina asked.

The team stopped. They moved the shelf closer to the wall. The change took ten minutes, and Mohsin complained about lifting it twice. When a younger child entered later, however, the path was clear and the books were within reach.

Sheikh Uncle came to inspect the result. He praised the teamwork, then read a line from Sūrah Ṣād. Allah reminds us of Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb as people of strength and insight. “Those words are far richer than muscles or clever guesses,” he explained. “They refer to noble capacity directed toward obedience and understanding.”
Mohsin looked at his hands. “Then lifting the shelf was not enough.”
“Useful strength requires good judgment,” Imaan answered.

Sheikh Uncle asked them to consider why the Qur’an praises these Prophets. They had strength in doing what Allah commanded, insight concerning guidance, and concern for the life to come. Their sacred qualities did not arise from earning a school prize. Our little project could only help us practise a separate, smaller lesson: see a real need, then work to meet it well.

Akhlaq looked over the room. One shelf leaned slightly. A few books were too high for the smallest readers. The team corrected both problems without waiting for another inspection. He began to understand that noticing a problem was a gift, and so was having the ability to correct it.
As they left, a child ran back to ask for a book about animals. Akhlaq showed the child the correct shelf, then stayed long enough to help choose something readable.
That evening he wrote beneath the family tree: HANDS TO HELP. EYES TO NOTICE.
The compass remained ordinary. Yet the words seemed to point somewhere: faith was not only something a person could describe. Its lessons should appear in the way a person saw others and acted.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Real ability combines useful work with wise attention.

stories.title: The Empty Chair at the Table
stories.subtitle: Leadership begins with worship and care

blocks.text: One Friday evening, Salaam invited the cousins for dinner. Dadi Jaan arranged the chairs while Imaan laid out plates. She left one chair near the end of the table empty.
“Who is sitting there?” Akhlaq asked.
“Someone we should not forget,” Dadi replied. “An elderly neighbour will join us after Maghrib. The walk is short, but she cannot carry heavy things.”

Mohsin offered to collect the guest’s meal. Mohsina set a glass of water nearby. Akhlaq moved a chair so the guest would not have to step around a crowded corner. None of them was a family leader in the ordinary adult sense, yet each had noticed a responsibility.

Later, Salaam reminded them of the Qur’an’s description of Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb. Allah made them leaders who guided by His command and inspired them toward good deeds, prayer and giving. “Their Prophethood is not something we imitate as a role,” he explained. “We learn from the guidance Allah revealed about them.”

The children had expected a lesson about being the loudest or the person with the most authority. Instead, Salaam asked simple questions. Had they remembered prayer in the excitement of preparing dinner? Had they treated the guest with dignity? Had anyone taken credit for work that another person performed?

Akhlaq confessed that he had nearly announced, “I planned the entire table,” although Imaan had done most of the arrangement. Mohsina raised an eyebrow, and everyone smiled. He corrected himself. “I planned one chair.”

The guest arrived and was welcomed without fuss. There was no formal speech about kindness. People listened when she spoke. They offered food without crowding her. When she left, they helped her return safely.

Afterwards Dadi asked which action had made the evening successful. Mohsin said carrying the things. Imaan said remembering the guest’s needs. Mohsina said asking what she wanted rather than assuming. Akhlaq said remembering not to boast.
“All of these matter,” Dadi answered. “But the foundation is remembering Allah and responding to His guidance.”

Before bed, Imaan placed the chair back under the table. It was only a chair, yet it had reminded her of a larger truth. A family’s worth was not proved by its impressive name. It appeared in sincere worship, generous care and the obligations people fulfilled when nobody demanded applause.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Leadership becomes beautiful through worship and service.
The next mystery arrived without a locked box or hidden letter. It came when Akhlaq rushed into the sitting room carrying a notebook with a bright drawing of stars and a moon.
“Look!” he announced. “I’ve drawn the dream Yūsuf told his father.”
Dadi Jaan glanced at the drawing. “Tell me what the Qur’an actually says before you add anything.”

Akhlaq opened Sūrah Yūsuf. The young Yūsuf described a dream of eleven stars, the sun and the moon, all prostrating to him. His father, Prophet Yaʿqūb, replied with careful advice that he should not tell this particular dream to his brothers, warning of possible plotting. The passage also speaks of Allah’s wisdom and His favour upon the family.
“Why would a father tell his child not to share news?” Imaan asked.
“Not all information belongs in every conversation,” Salaam replied. “Yaʿqūb knew a danger that needed wise care. He was protecting his son, not encouraging falsehood.”

That afternoon at school, Mohsina quietly told Imaan she felt nervous about a class presentation. “Please don’t tell everybody,” she said. Imaan promised to keep the matter private, but later another pupil asked why Mohsina seemed so quiet.
Imaan paused. A simple truthful answer was enough: “She is preparing for the presentation.” There was no reason to reveal a friend’s worry.

Akhlaq thought this meant secrets should always be kept. Sheikh Uncle corrected him gently. “Ordinary privacy is different from a secret about danger, harm, abuse or a threat. A child must tell a trustworthy adult when someone is unsafe, even if another child says, ‘Don’t tell.’”

Back at home, Imaan explained to Akhlaq that a wise person knows when to speak, when not to share another person’s private matter, and when safety requires help. The Qur’an’s specific account was a prophetic father protecting his son from danger. Their modern school lesson concerned respectful trust and safe communication; it was not a reenactment of sacred history.
The following morning, Mohsina completed her presentation. Imaan congratulated her without describing the nervous moments to the class. Mohsina noticed and quietly thanked her.
That evening, Akhlaq amended his notebook title. Instead of THE SECRET OF THE ELEVEN STARS, he wrote A TRUSTED CONVERSATION. The stars had not changed. What he understood about trust had.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Trust includes discretion and knowing when safety requires adult help.

stories.title: The Report That Did Not Explain Everything
stories.subtitle: Beautiful patience does not deny reality

blocks.text: The school’s inter-class science exhibition was nearly ready when a glass display panel cracked. Nobody was injured, but the organisers were upset. Two pupils said they knew who had broken it. Their stories did not match, and a younger child was becoming the centre of the whispers.
Akhlaq wanted the matter settled immediately. “Someone must have done it,” he said. “We should ask everyone until they confess.”
Sir Zameer stopped him. “We should establish what happened, keep everyone safe and avoid accusing without evidence. Pressure is not the same as truth.”

The children examined the area with their teacher. They learned that the panel had not been secured correctly and had cracked after being moved. The younger pupil had not caused the damage. Akhlaq apologised for repeating the rumour.

During the afternoon lesson, Sir Zameer read Sūrah Yūsuf 12:18. The brothers had come with a shirt stained by false blood, and Yaʿqūb recognised that what they described was not the truth. He sought beautiful patience and Allah’s help.

The classroom became quiet. The teacher did not compare a cracked display panel with the terrible pain of separation from a child. That would have made the Prophetic account seem ordinary. Instead, he showed a limited character lesson: when people bring troubling information, we should not turn fear into unfair accusations; patience can include seeking the truth and asking Allah for help.

Imaan asked whether beautiful patience meant that Yaʿqūb had never been sad. Sir Zameer explained that the Qur’an plainly describes his grief. Patience was not pretending a loss did not hurt. It was refusing to abandon reliance upon Allah amid pain.

At home, Akhlaq looked back at the cracked panel. He had been eager to blame someone because not knowing had felt uncomfortable. He wrote one sentence: WHEN I DO NOT KNOW, I MUST NOT INVENT AN ANSWER.

The teacher arranged a safer display for the exhibition, and the children helped move the projects. The incident ended without a dramatic confession or a grand prize. But one younger student returned to the classroom the next day without the unfair rumour hanging over him. That mattered more than finishing the story quickly.

Akhlaq placed a small card under the family tree: PATIENCE WITH TRUTH. Beside it he left space for the next card, wondering whether patience could survive not merely an afternoon’s confusion, but years of disappointment. Dadi Jaan promised that Yaʿqūb’s story had more to teach them.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Patience protects the truth while seeking Allah’s help.

stories.title: The Hope Notebook
stories.subtitle: When sorrow and trust stand together

blocks.text: There was an empty space on the noticeboard at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy, where the children had planned to display thank-you notes to people who quietly supported the school. It stayed empty because one of their teachers was absent due to a family difficulty.
Imaan suggested postponing the whole project. “It feels wrong to celebrate when somebody is struggling,” she said.
Mohsina thought for a moment. “Could we make room for care instead of simply cancelling everything?”

They asked their teacher what support would be appropriate. He suggested a brief respectful card, without asking for private details and without sharing the family’s circumstances with other students. Together they wrote a note offering kind wishes and practical help when needed.

That evening, Akhlaq told Dadi Jaan he wished every hard situation could be solved by a thoughtful card. Dadi agreed that the world did not work that way. Even prophets faced grief. In Sūrah Yūsuf, Yaʿqūb spoke of his sorrow and distress and directed his complaint to Allah. Then he instructed his sons to search for Yūsuf and his brother and not to despair of Allah’s relief.
“Was he unhappy with Allah?” Akhlaq asked.
“No,” Dadi said. “He was deeply grieved, yet he continued to turn to Allah. Feeling sadness is not proof of weak faith.”

Imaan looked at her notebook. She had written three words for a class presentation: HOPE, PATIENCE, ACTION. She had expected the three words to describe cheerful people who never cried. Now she understood that they mattered most precisely when something was hard.

The following week, the teacher returned briefly to thank the class. He did not tell the children every detail of his family situation. Nobody pressed him for information. The children had offered what they could: discretion, a useful task completed without him, and the willingness to help.

Mohsin asked whether hope guaranteed that the teacher’s situation would improve quickly. Salaam explained that belief in Allah’s mercy does not give us knowledge of a particular worldly outcome. We seek help, make duʿāʾ, and do what is right without claiming to control the result.
Akhlaq added a new page to his notebook titled WHEN I FEEL SAD. He wrote: Pray. Speak to a trusted adult. Ask for help. Do one useful thing that is within my power.
Dadi approved, but added one more line: YOU MAY NEED REST, TOO. Care did not demand a constant smile.

That night the family tree rested beneath the notebook. Its names reminded the children that Allah’s chosen servants were not spared every hardship. They were honoured for faithful guidance through it.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Grief, duʿāʾ and practical effort can coexist.

stories.title: The Question Worth Leaving Behind
stories.subtitle: A family legacy written through choices

blocks.text: On the final day of their learning week, the school held a modest family gathering. Instead of a stage competition, each class would present one lesson that could improve life at home. Imaan and Akhlaq brought their family-tree poster, now crowded with notes: GRATITUDE. SINCERE WORSHIP. WISE COUNSEL. BEAUTIFUL PATIENCE. HOPE WITH ACTION.
Mohsin was convinced they needed a dramatic title. “THE GREATEST FAMILY TREE IN HISTORY!” he suggested.
Imaan smiled. “We are not ranking families, Mohsin. We are learning from Prophets honoured by Allah.”

Sheikh Uncle asked them to choose one Qur’anic scene to conclude the exhibition. They selected Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:133. The verse speaks of Yaʿqūb asking his sons, as death approached, whom they would worship after him. They affirmed that they would worship the One God of Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl and Isḥāq, and submit to Him.
Akhlaq first thought the lesson was about remembering names. Then Dadi asked, “What did Yaʿqūb actually ask?”
He looked down. “Whom they would worship.”
“That,” said Dadi, “was the heart of the legacy. Family honour did not rest on inherited labels. The children needed to hold sincerely to Tawḥīd themselves.”

Salamah reminded them that younger children should be loved and taught with kindness, not tested publicly about their hearts. Nobody could measure someone’s īmān through a school worksheet. They could, however, help one another remember prayer, tell the truth, keep promises and treat people justly.

As guests visited their table, Imaan asked each family to choose one small practice they wanted to carry forward. A father chose to listen without interrupting. A mother chose to set aside time to read the Qur’an with her children. One older brother promised to help a younger sibling with homework. A grandmother chose to make a weekly call to a relative who lived far away.

Akhlaq wrote each idea on a paper leaf and attached it to a large branch. By afternoon the display was filled with ordinary actions. Nothing flashed. No mysterious door opened. The beauty of it lay in what people had freely decided to do.
After the gathering, Dadi Jaan handed Imaan one final blank card. On it were the words: THE NEXT STORY BEGINS WITH A DREAM.
Akhlaq looked up immediately. “Yūsuf?”
Dadi smiled. “In shāʾ Allāh. But before we follow his story, remember his father. A family’s greatest gift is not its fame, but its faithful guidance.”

They placed the card beside the names ISḤĀQ and YAʿQŪB. The compass lay nearby, motionless. This time Akhlaq did not try to make it glow. He understood that the most important direction was already there in the words they had chosen to practise.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: The lasting legacy of faith is chosen and practised, not merely inherited.

missions.title: A Blessing Across Generations

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Explain that Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb were gifts from Allah and that gratitude does not promise knowledge of the future.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Hūd, 11:71: The wife of Ibrāhīm received glad tidings of Isḥāq, and after Isḥāq, of Yaʿqūb.
وَامْرَأَتُهُ قَائِمَةٌ فَضَحِكَتْ فَبَشَّرْنَاهَا بِإِسْحَاقَ وَمِنْ وَرَاءِ إِسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The Qur’an places the good news in Ibrāhīm’s household. Isḥāq’s Prophethood and the future blessing of Yaʿqūb are gifts from Allah, not a rule that every family can predict its future.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: When did I turn hope into a promise I could not guarantee?

missions.question: Your cousin has received happy news and announces that everything in the family will now be perfect.

choices.text: Congratulate the family, thank Allah, and avoid promising an unknown future.
choices.feedback: Good news should be met with gratitude and wise hope. We do not control the unseen or guarantee worldly outcomes.

choices.text: Agree that success will always continue.
choices.feedback: No one can promise a flawless future; offer gratitude and commitments you can actually keep. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Ignore the news because not every day will be happy.
choices.feedback: Good news should not be ignored. Celebrate kindly without claiming knowledge of the unseen. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Congratulate one person sincerely today and make a duʿāʾ for their wellbeing without making a prediction.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: When did I turn hope into a promise I could not guarantee? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.text: بُشْرَى (glad tidings), وَهَبْنَا (We bestowed)

missions.title: Family Honour Is Not a Race

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Recognize that nobility of lineage is no excuse for pride, and individual conduct matters.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Ṣāffāt, 37:113: Allah blessed Ibrāhīm and Isḥāq; their descendants would include both those who do good and those who wrong themselves.
وَبَارَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَىٰ إِسْحَاقَ ۚ وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِهِمَا مُحْسِنٌ وَظَالِمٌ لِنَفْسِهِ مُبِينٌ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Allah praised these Prophets, but 37:113 explicitly distinguishes righteous and wrongdoing descendants. Human worth and responsibility do not follow automatically from ancestry.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Am I impressed by a name more than by conduct?

missions.question: Two classmates argue that the child from a famous family must be a better leader.

choices.text: Choose the famous name without asking about behaviour.
choices.feedback: A family reputation is not a substitute for the candidate’s real conduct. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Evaluate the actual responsibility, honesty and ability of all candidates.
choices.feedback: The Qur’an itself says descendants can act differently. A family name neither replaces righteousness nor removes the duty to behave well.

choices.text: Assume children from well-known families can never be trusted.
choices.feedback: It is equally unfair to treat someone badly simply because their family is famous. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Praise a person for one sincere action rather than wealth, popularity or family background.

missions.title: Three Generations, One Guidance

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Identify Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb correctly and describe continuity of Tawḥīd.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Anbiyāʾ, 21:72: Allah granted Ibrāhīm Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, and made each righteous.
وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ إِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ نَافِلَةً ۖ وَكُلًّا جَعَلْنَا صَالِحِينَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The Qur’an names a true family relationship and a succession of guidance. Accuracy matters; our family-tree exercise is only a way to remember that Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb were Prophets.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I use knowledge to help or to display superiority?

missions.question: A younger child confuses Ismāʿīl and Yaʿqūb and asks you to help with a family chart.

choices.text: Replace the chart with a list of your favourite prophets.
choices.feedback: An accurate chart teaches the actual relationships, not a list of favourites. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Explain the relationships kindly, check the verse and let the child fill the chart.
choices.feedback: Accurate learning is an act of respect. Teach gently, distinguish relatives correctly, and let the learner grow.

choices.text: Laugh and say everyone should already know.
choices.feedback: A learner should never be humiliated for asking about a family relationship. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Help someone learn one fact patiently; allow them to try it without doing everything for them.

missions.title: Hands to Serve, Eyes to Notice

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Explain that strength and insight support faithful action and wise responsibility.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Ṣād, 38:45: Remember Allah’s servants Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, people of strength and insight.
وَاذْكُرْ عِبَادَنَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ أُولِي الْأَيْدِي وَالْأَبْصَارِ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The Qur’an commends strength and insight in Allah’s chosen servants. We must not translate their Prophetic rank into a classroom talent contest. Our school project illustrates only a practical moral application.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Did I see an unmet need that I could reasonably help with?

missions.question: Your team finishes a school project, but the display blocks access for a younger child.

choices.text: Leave it; your team worked hard.
choices.feedback: Hard work does not justify blocking access or ignoring another person’s needs. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Criticize the child for needing room.
choices.feedback: The child seeking access deserves dignity, not criticism. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Notice the access problem and improve the display even if it takes more effort.
choices.feedback: Useful ability joins effort with understanding. A project matters most when it serves people without harm.

missions.action: Notice one small difficulty another person faces and make a practical improvement within your ability.

missions.title: A Leader Who Remembers Worship

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Understand that Prophetic leadership in revelation combined guidance, good deeds, prayer and giving.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Anbiyāʾ, 21:73: Allah made them leaders guiding by His command; they practised goodness, prayer, giving, and worship.
وَجَعَلْنَاهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْهِمْ فِعْلَ الْخَيْرَاتِ وَإِقَامَ الصَّلَاةِ وَإِيتَاءَ الزَّكَاةِ ۖ وَكَانُوا لَنَا عَابِدِينَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Guidance, good deeds, prayer, giving and worship occur together in the description of Prophetic leadership. In everyday life children can serve others without claiming sacred status.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Have I treated a position as a service or as a privilege?

missions.question: A team captain wants to win but refuses to help with equipment or give fair turns.

choices.text: Take away every decision from the captain.
choices.feedback: Taking every decision away from the captain prevents teamwork and learning. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Agree that being captain means avoiding small duties.
choices.feedback: Leadership brings duties; avoiding them is a misuse of responsibility. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Encourage fair turns, service and respect for prayer and responsibilities.
choices.feedback: Our modern leadership tasks are not prophethood. They can, however, become places to practise service and sincerity.

missions.action: Complete one small helpful task without asking to be publicly thanked.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: Have I treated a position as a service or as a privilege? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: أَئِمَّة (leaders), الْخَيْرَات (good deeds)

missions.title: What Will Outlast the Trophy?

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Distinguish lasting faith and service from brief recognition.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-ʿAnkabūt, 29:27: Allah gave Ibrāhīm Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb and placed prophethood and scripture among his descendants.
وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ إِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي ذُرِّيَّتِهِ النُّبُوَّةَ وَالْكِتَابَ وَآتَيْنَاهُ أَجْرَهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا ۖ وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Allah’s grant of prophethood and scripture among Ibrāhīm’s descendants illustrates a long religious legacy. Our short-term prizes fade; sincere guidance and responsibility matter more.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: What could someone benefit from after my praise has faded?

missions.question: You are given a certificate, but a younger pupil asks you to explain how to participate next year.

choices.text: Enjoy the certificate gratefully and help the younger pupil learn.
choices.feedback: Excellence is not forbidden. It becomes richer when achievement makes someone more thankful and useful.

choices.text: Throw away your certificate to prove you are humble.
choices.feedback: Humility does not require despising a legitimate achievement. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Say that only winners deserve your time.
choices.feedback: Knowledge and success become more meaningful when shared rather than guarded. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Share one useful tip with someone who is beginning a skill you have already learned.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: What could someone benefit from after my praise has faded? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: الْكِتَاب (Scripture), الدَّار (the final abode)

missions.title: A Trusted Conversation

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Recognize wise parental counsel and distinguish ordinary privacy from unsafe secrecy.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Yūsuf, 12:4: Young Yūsuf told his father of a remarkable dream involving eleven stars, the sun and the moon.
إِذْ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَا أَبَتِ إِنِّي رَأَيْتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا وَالشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ رَأَيْتُهُمْ لِي سَاجِدِينَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Young Yūsuf confided his extraordinary dream to Yaʿqūb; the father gave situation-specific advice. The lesson is care and wise trust, not a general ban on sharing feelings.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: What is the difference between a private feeling and a dangerous secret?

missions.question: A friend tells you that they feel nervous about a presentation and asks for discretion.

choices.text: Tell the entire class so everyone can discuss it.
choices.feedback: Sharing a friend’s ordinary worry without consent breaks trust. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Respect the friend’s privacy and offer support; seek adult help if anyone is unsafe.
choices.feedback: The Qur’anic scene concerns Yaʿqūb’s specific advice to Yūsuf. In school, trust means gentle discretion; danger must be shared with responsible adults.

choices.text: Promise to keep all secrets even if someone is being harmed.
choices.feedback: Never promise absolute secrecy when somebody may be unsafe or harmed. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Respect one harmless private matter today and ask a trusted adult for help whenever safety is involved.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: What is the difference between a private feeling and a dangerous secret? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: يَا أَبَتِ (O my father), رُؤْيَا (dream/vision)

missions.title: Wisdom Before Sharing

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Use care when passing on news, especially when it may cause hurt or jealousy.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Yūsuf, 12:5: Yaʿqūb advised his son not to disclose this particular dream to his brothers, warning of possible plotting.
قَالَ يَا بُنَيَّ لَا تَقْصُصْ رُؤْيَاكَ عَلَىٰ إِخْوَتِكَ فَيَكِيدُوا لَكَ كَيْدًا ۖ إِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Yaʿqūb warned against plotting in a particular family situation. Contemporary prudence means checking information, protecting dignity and telling adults when there is danger.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Have I exposed someone else’s private news for attention?

missions.question: A class group chat contains an exciting rumour about another pupil’s future award.

choices.text: Forward it to increase excitement.
choices.feedback: A rumour can harm someone even when it sounds exciting. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Create a second rumour to test who believes it.
choices.feedback: Spreading a new rumour creates confusion rather than verifying the truth. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Do not circulate an unverified or private claim; ask responsibly if needed.
choices.feedback: Prudence does not mean fear of everyone. It means paying attention to context, reliability and another person’s dignity.

missions.action: Before sharing one message today, ask whether it is true, necessary and kind.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: Have I exposed someone else’s private news for attention? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: كَيْد (plot), عَلِيم (All-Knowing)

missions.title: Beautiful Patience and Evidence

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Explain that beautiful patience coexists with grief, seeking help and refusal to accuse without evidence.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Yūsuf, 12:18: Faced with a false account of Yūsuf’s fate, Yaʿqūb held to beautiful patience and sought Allah’s help.
وَجَاءُوا عَلَىٰ قَمِيصِهِ بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ ۚ قَالَ بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ أَنْفُسُكُمْ أَمْرًا ۖ فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ ۖ وَاللَّهُ الْمُسْتَعَانُ عَلَىٰ مَا تَصِفُونَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: The Qur’an shows Yaʿqūb encountering a false account and turning to beautiful patience. This is profound familial grief, not a trivial school setback; we practise only the limited lesson about truth and fairness.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: When uncertainty makes me anxious, do I invent an explanation?

missions.question: A valuable school display is damaged, and a child is blamed before the facts are checked.

choices.text: Report facts calmly, protect people from rumours and ask the teacher to investigate.
choices.feedback: Yaʿqūb’s trial was far more serious than a school incident. A limited modern lesson is to avoid unjust blame while seeking Allah’s help.

choices.text: Repeat the accusation quickly.
choices.feedback: Unverified accusations can wound an innocent child. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Hide the damage forever to avoid disagreement.
choices.feedback: Quietly hiding damage is not the same as learning the truth and putting things right. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Stop one rumour or unfair accusation by saying, “We should check before blaming.”

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: When uncertainty makes me anxious, do I invent an explanation? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: صَبْرٌ جَمِيل (beautiful patience), الْمُسْتَعَان (the One whose help is sought)

missions.title: Sorrow Is Not a Failure of Faith

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Learn that prophets could experience grief while turning sincerely to Allah.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Yūsuf, 12:86: Yaʿqūb says he pours his anguish and sorrow out to Allah.
قَالَ إِنَّمَا أَشْكُو بَثِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَى اللَّهِ وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Yaʿqūb openly described grief while turning to Allah. A child may feel sad, seek comfort and request help; we must not diagnose another person’s faith by their tears.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I make space for grief without forcing cheerful words?

missions.question: Someone in your family is sad. A friend says they should simply stop crying if they trust Allah.

choices.text: Demand that they describe every detail of their pain to you.
choices.feedback: Do not press someone to expose private pain in order to receive your kindness. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Listen kindly, make duʿāʾ and help them seek appropriate family or professional support.
choices.feedback: Yaʿqūb’s words show grief and devotion together. Children need permission to feel, speak and receive appropriate care.

choices.text: Agree that crying always means weak faith.
choices.feedback: Grief does not by itself indicate weak faith. Yaʿqūb turned to Allah while grieving. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Offer quiet listening or one safe practical help to someone dealing with difficulty; respect their privacy.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: Do I make space for grief without forcing cheerful words? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: حُزْن (grief), أَشْكُو (I complain/entrust my distress)

missions.title: Hope That Takes a Step

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Recognize that hope in Allah and responsible action can accompany one another.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Yūsuf, 12:87: Yaʿqūb instructed his sons to search for Yūsuf and his brother and never despair of Allah’s relief.
يَا بَنِيَّ اذْهَبُوا فَتَحَسَّسُوا مِنْ يُوسُفَ وَأَخِيهِ وَلَا تَيْأَسُوا مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّهُ لَا يَيْأَسُ مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا الْقَوْمُ الْكَافِرُونَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Yaʿqūb instructed his sons to search rather than surrender to despair. Hope does not guarantee that every outcome will happen immediately, and wise action remains our responsibility.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Which useful next action is within my control today?

missions.question: A missing schoolbook matters to the class, but the first search fails.

choices.text: Give up immediately and accuse whoever last entered.
choices.feedback: Abandoning a responsible search and blaming others is neither patient nor fair. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Promise the class that a miracle will bring it back by tomorrow.
choices.feedback: Hope means trusting Allah while acting responsibly, not promising miracles on a schedule. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Make a calm search plan, ask the responsible adult and remain hopeful without claiming certainty.
choices.feedback: Yaʿqūb told his sons to make an effort while forbidding despair. Hope is not an excuse to do nothing or pretend to know outcomes.

missions.action: Take one practical step toward a responsibility you have been postponing, asking for help when needed.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: Which useful next action is within my control today? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: تَحَسَّسُوا (inquire/search), رَوْحِ اللَّه (Allah’s relief/mercy)

missions.title: The Faith We Leave Behind

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Explain that Yaʿqūb’s final concern was worship of the One God and faithful continuity.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Al-Baqarah, 2:133: Yaʿqūb asked his children whom they would worship after him; they affirmed worship of the One God and submission to Him.

أَمْ كُنْتُمْ شُهَدَاءَ إِذْ حَضَرَ يَعْقُوبَ الْمَوْتُ إِذْ قَالَ لِبَنِيهِ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ بَعْدِي قَالُوا نَعْبُدُ إِلَٰهَكَ وَإِلَٰهَ آبَائِكَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ إِلَٰهًا وَاحِدًا وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Yaʿqūb’s final concern in the Qur’an is Tawḥīd. His children respond with their own affirmation of faith. A family’s legacy is a call to sincere guidance, not inherited entitlement.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: What good practice would I like to make easier for the next generation?

missions.question: Your family is planning a weekly learning time, but people disagree on what will make it sustainable.

choices.text: Agree on a small, welcoming routine based on Qur’an, worship and good character.
choices.feedback: The Qur’an records the children’s own affirmation of Tawḥīd. Family faith is taught with sincere example, not measured by an app leaderboard.

choices.text: Declare that the family’s name alone proves its faith.
choices.feedback: Family names do not replace sincere worship or individual moral choices. Review the verse and try again.

choices.text: Choose complicated rules and punish anyone who misses a day.
choices.feedback: Complexity and shame can drive families away from a gentle sustainable practice. Review the verse and try again.

missions.action: Agree on one small voluntary family practice, such as reading a short passage or helping someone each week.

remember.text: What good practice would I like to make easier for the next generation? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip”, without a public score.

remember.label: Vocabulary
remember.text: نَعْبُدُ (we worship), مُسْلِمُون (those who submit)

review.arabic: وَامْرَأَتُهُ قَائِمَةٌ فَضَحِكَتْ فَبَشَّرْنَاهَا بِإِسْحَاقَ وَمِنْ وَرَاءِ إِسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبَ
review.meaning: The wife of Ibrāhīm received glad tidings of Isḥāq, and after Isḥāq, of Yaʿqūb.

review.arabic: وَبَشَّرْنَاهُ بِإِسْحَاقَ نَبِيًّا مِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
review.meaning: Allah gave Ibrāhīm glad tidings of Isḥāq, a prophet among the righteous.

review.arabic: وَبَارَكْنَا عَلَيْهِ وَعَلَىٰ إِسْحَاقَ ۚ وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِهِمَا مُحْسِنٌ وَظَالِمٌ لِنَفْسِهِ مُبِينٌ
review.meaning: Allah blessed Ibrāhīm and Isḥāq; their descendants would include both those who do good and those who wrong themselves.

review.arabic: وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ إِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ نَافِلَةً ۖ وَكُلًّا جَعَلْنَا صَالِحِينَ
review.meaning: Allah granted Ibrāhīm Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, and made each righteous.

review.arabic: وَجَعَلْنَاهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا وَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَيْهِمْ فِعْلَ الْخَيْرَاتِ وَإِقَامَ الصَّلَاةِ وَإِيتَاءَ الزَّكَاةِ ۖ وَكَانُوا لَنَا عَابِدِينَ
review.meaning: Allah made them leaders guiding by His command; they practised goodness, prayer, giving, and worship.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّا اعْتَزَلَهُمْ وَمَا يَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ وَهَبْنَا لَهُ إِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ ۖ وَكُلًّا جَعَلْنَا نَبِيًّا
review.meaning: After Ibrāhīm separated from false worship, Allah bestowed Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, and made each a prophet.

review.arabic: وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ إِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَجَعَلْنَا فِي ذُرِّيَّتِهِ النُّبُوَّةَ وَالْكِتَابَ وَآتَيْنَاهُ أَجْرَهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا ۖ وَإِنَّهُ فِي الْآخِرَةِ لَمِنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
review.meaning: Allah gave Ibrāhīm Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb and placed prophethood and scripture among his descendants.

review.arabic: وَاذْكُرْ عِبَادَنَا إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ أُولِي الْأَيْدِي وَالْأَبْصَارِ
review.meaning: Remember Allah’s servants Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb, people of strength and insight.

review.arabic: إِنَّا أَخْلَصْنَاهُمْ بِخَالِصَةٍ ذِكْرَى الدَّارِ
review.meaning: Allah distinguished them through sincere remembrance of the final abode.

review.arabic: وَإِنَّهُمْ عِنْدَنَا لَمِنَ الْمُصْطَفَيْنَ الْأَخْيَارِ
review.meaning: They are among those Allah chose, among the excellent.

review.arabic: وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعْقُوبُ يَا بَنِيَّ إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَىٰ لَكُمُ الدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm and Yaʿqūb urged their children to remain devoted to Allah and to die in submission to Him.

review.arabic: أَمْ كُنْتُمْ شُهَدَاءَ إِذْ حَضَرَ يَعْقُوبَ الْمَوْتُ إِذْ قَالَ لِبَنِيهِ مَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ بَعْدِي قَالُوا نَعْبُدُ إِلَٰهَكَ وَإِلَٰهَ آبَائِكَ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ إِلَٰهًا وَاحِدًا وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb asked his children whom they would worship after him; they affirmed worship of the One God and submission to Him.

review.arabic: إِذْ قَالَ يُوسُفُ لِأَبِيهِ يَا أَبَتِ إِنِّي رَأَيْتُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ كَوْكَبًا وَالشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ رَأَيْتُهُمْ لِي سَاجِدِينَ
review.meaning: Young Yūsuf told his father of a remarkable dream involving eleven stars, the sun and the moon.

review.arabic: قَالَ يَا بُنَيَّ لَا تَقْصُصْ رُؤْيَاكَ عَلَىٰ إِخْوَتِكَ فَيَكِيدُوا لَكَ كَيْدًا ۖ إِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb advised his son not to disclose this particular dream to his brothers, warning of possible plotting.

review.arabic: وَكَذَٰلِكَ يَجْتَبِيكَ رَبُّكَ وَيُعَلِّمُكَ مِنْ تَأْوِيلِ الْأَحَادِيثِ وَيُتِمُّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَىٰ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ كَمَا أَتَمَّهَا عَلَىٰ أَبَوَيْكَ مِنْ قَبْلُ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْحَاقَ ۚ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ عَلِيمٌ حَكِيمٌ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb described Allah’s knowledge, wisdom and favour reaching his family through the prophetic legacy.

review.arabic: وَجَاءُوا عَلَىٰ قَمِيصِهِ بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ ۚ قَالَ بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ أَنْفُسُكُمْ أَمْرًا ۖ فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ ۖ وَاللَّهُ الْمُسْتَعَانُ عَلَىٰ مَا تَصِفُونَ
review.meaning: Faced with a false account of Yūsuf’s fate, Yaʿqūb held to beautiful patience and sought Allah’s help.

review.arabic: قَالَ بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ أَنْفُسُكُمْ أَمْرًا ۖ فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ ۖ عَسَى اللَّهُ أَنْ يَأْتِيَنِي بِهِمْ جَمِيعًا ۚ إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ
review.meaning: In further family trial, Yaʿqūb again held to beautiful patience and hope in Allah’s knowledge and wisdom.

review.arabic: قَالَ إِنَّمَا أَشْكُو بَثِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَى اللَّهِ وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb says he pours his anguish and sorrow out to Allah.

review.arabic: يَا بَنِيَّ اذْهَبُوا فَتَحَسَّسُوا مِنْ يُوسُفَ وَأَخِيهِ وَلَا تَيْأَسُوا مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّهُ لَا يَيْأَسُ مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا الْقَوْمُ الْكَافِرُونَ
review.meaning: Yaʿqūb instructed his sons to search for Yūsuf and his brother and never despair of Allah’s relief.

review.arabic: فَلَمَّا أَنْ جَاءَ الْبَشِيرُ أَلْقَاهُ عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ فَارْتَدَّ بَصِيرًا ۖ قَالَ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكُمْ إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
review.meaning: The bearer of good news came, and by Allah’s decree Yaʿqūb’s sight returned as the Qur’an recounts.

review.arabic: قَالُوا يَا أَبَانَا اسْتَغْفِرْ لَنَا ذُنُوبَنَا إِنَّا كُنَّا خَاطِئِينَ
review.meaning: The sons asked their father to seek forgiveness for them after acknowledging wrongdoing.

review.arabic: قَالَ سَوْفَ أَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكُمْ رَبِّي ۖ إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ
review.meaning: Their father promised to seek his Lord’s forgiveness for them, affirming Allah as Forgiving and Merciful.

synthesis.text: The blessing did not end with a birth

The Qur’anic introduction to Isḥāq begins with a gift. His arrival is announced as glad tidings to the household of Ibrāhīm, and he is praised as a prophet and one of the righteous. The revelation also identifies Yaʿqūb in the next generation. The lesson is not that famous families are automatically successful. The Qur’an itself distinguishes those who do good from those who wrong themselves. Blessings make gratitude and accountability more necessary, not less.
Faith joined insight and service

The Qur’an describes Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb as possessors of strength and insight. It also describes guidance by Allah’s command, righteous actions, established prayer, giving and worship. The correct response is not to invent exciting biographies where revelation gives no details, but to understand how deeply faith, knowledge, worship and responsible action belong together. Modern children may practise attentiveness, work, service and truthfulness in age-appropriate settings. Such lessons are not claims of similarity in sacred rank.
The father who knew sorrow and still hoped

Yaʿqūb appears memorably as a father: he listens to Yūsuf, offers protective counsel and later bears severe family grief. The Qur’an records his beautiful patience, his frank words about sorrow and his reliance on Allah. It then records his insistence that his sons should search and should not despair. This combination matters greatly for children. Sadness is not a moral failure. Patience is not silence about harm. Hope does not require pretending that a problem does not exist. A caring family listens, seeks appropriate help and continues to act responsibly.
The last question was about worship

In al-Baqarah 2:133, Yaʿqūb’s concern as death approached was not how many trophies his descendants would collect, but whom they would worship. The sons affirmed the One God. The enduring legacy was Tawḥīd and submission to Allah, accompanied by a duty to practise the faith with sincerity. The Imaan & Akhlaq app must preserve that theological centre, even while teaching practical kindness, reliability, humility and family care.
CARRY FORWARD • Remember the Giver. Serve with what you receive. Protect the truth. Ask for help in sorrow. Keep hope alive through responsible action. Worship Allah sincerely.
